opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think people really underestimate how much of AI progress is just the accumulation of a lot of small, unglamorous changes. From the outside it looks like there are these big discrete jumps, like a new model drops and suddenly everything is better. But inside, it's usually hundreds of little things stacked on top of each other: a slightly better data mixture, a tweak to the learning rate schedule, fixing some tokenizer issue, changing the activation function, being more careful about initialization, better filtering. Each of those might give you a fraction of a percent, and individually none of them would make a nice paper. But compounded together, you get something that looks like a step change.

I've always felt the research community is a bit biased toward novelty, toward the big new idea with a fancy name. That's understandable, because that's what gets attention. But a lot of the real gains come from people who are willing to do careful ablations and sweat the details. It's more engineering-flavored, and some people look down on it a bit, but I think it's actually where a huge amount of the value is.

There's also a flip side: a lot of "incremental improvements" that get published don't really hold up at scale. Something works at a small scale on one benchmark, and when you try it in a large training run it either washes out or actually hurts. So part of the skill is developing taste for which small changes are real and which are noise. That only comes from running a lot of experiments and getting burned a few times.

So my view is that big ideas matter, like the Transformer obviously mattered a lot, but the day-to-day reality of progress is much more about steady compounding. The teams that do well are the ones that are disciplined about stacking many small wins without breaking things along the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI progress comes from “hundreds of little things stacked on top of each other” that compound into an apparent step change.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I actually have kind of a nuanced take on this. I think people underestimate how much of progress is just, like, a lot of small things stacking up. When I was at Google Brain working on things like PaLM and UL2 and all the architecture stuff, a lot of what actually mattered was not one big idea. It was, you know, this tweak to the optimizer, this change in how you do the data mixture, slightly better tokenization, a different learning rate schedule. Each of those is like a one or two percent thing, and nobody writes a paper about them individually, but if you compound twenty of those you end up with a model that's dramatically better.

At the same time, I'm a bit skeptical of the way incremental work shows up in the academic literature. There's this whole genre of papers where someone proposes a new attention variant or a new architecture and shows it beats the baseline by half a point on some benchmark. And a lot of that doesn't survive contact with scale. I wrote about this with the "Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures" work, where we found that a lot of these supposedly better architectures just don't hold up once you scale compute. So there's a difference between small changes that are genuinely robust and small changes that are basically noise that got through the review process.

The other thing I'd say is that the incremental stuff only works if you have the infrastructure and the discipline to actually measure it. Inside a frontier lab, you have good evals, you have reproducible training pipelines, you can run ablations at reasonable scale, and so you can actually tell which one percent gains are real. If you don't have that, you're kind of just guessing. And that's honestly one of the things I learned the hard way when I went off and started Reka. A lot of the "secret sauce" is not a secret, it's just hundreds of careful small decisions, and you have to be able to verify each one.

So I guess my view is: the big leaps like transformers or scaling get all the attention, and they deserve it, but the day-to-day reality of pushing the frontier is very much incremental. The skill is in knowing which increments are real.

r001.rationale: The candidate says progress comes from many small changes stacking up and explains that compounding them can make a model dramatically better.

astra-6.text:
I think small incremental changes are actually very important. We tend to tell the story of AI progress through big breakthroughs, but a lot of the work is getting many little things right—the data, the training recipe, the architecture, the evaluation. Each improvement might look modest on its own, but they can compound into something quite substantial.

The challenge is knowing whether an incremental change is teaching you something useful. If it gives you a slightly better number but you don’t understand why, it’s harder to build on. If it helps you understand what matters, then even a small result can point toward a much bigger idea.

r001.rationale: It says individually modest improvements can compound into something quite substantial.

sol-6.1.text:
I think small, incremental changes are really important. We tend to tell the story of AI progress through a few big breakthroughs, but a lot of the work is improving the data, getting the training recipe right, and understanding why one seemingly minor choice works better than another. Those improvements can compound.

At the same time, I think you have to distinguish between a change that moves a benchmark a little and a change that teaches us something. Even a small result can be valuable if it gives us a principle that carries over to other settings. The question is: what did we learn, and what does that let us do next?

r001.rationale: The response says small improvements across data, training recipes, and choices can compound, clearly conveying that accumulated incremental changes contribute to AI progress.
